title: The mind like the wind
hookLine: Arjuna says the mind can't be held; Krishna says practice and letting go can hold it
carry: abhyasa and vairagya: the self lifts the self
tomorrow: maya: illusion, or God's real power? who's right?

lines: THE MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.
cards: Halfway through the Gita's sixth chapter, Arjuna pushes back. Krishna has been teaching him to sit and steady the mind, and Arjuna says, more or less: I can't.
The mind is restless, stubborn, strong; holding it is as hard as holding the wind. Krishna doesn't argue. He agrees.
And earlier in that same chapter, he'd given a verse that seems stuck on one word: uddhared atmanatmanam. Atman, atman, atman. Why say self over and over?

teach.b: The answer is the word itself. Atman can mean the self in the big sense, or plain oneself, the way English says himself or herself, and this verse, Gita 6.5, uses both.
Uddhared atmanatmanam, natmanam avasadayet; atmaiva hy atmano bandhur, atmaiva ripur atmanah.

teach.h: LIFT THE SELF BY THE SELF.
teach.b: Let one lift the self by the self, and not sink the self; for the self alone is the self's friend, and the self alone its enemy. Bandhu, friend, also kin. Ripu, enemy.
The endings tell the shapes apart: atmana, by the self; atmanam, the self being lifted; atmanah, of the self.
The next verse explains: to one who has mastered himself, the self is a friend; to one who hasn't, it behaves like an enemy. Now the teaching, and this is Hindu yoga at its root.
When Arjuna says the mind is like the wind, Krishna answers: abhyasena tu kaunteya vairagyena cha grihyate.
It is held by abhyasa and by vairagya. Abhyasa, practice: coming back, again and again, to the chosen thing, a mantra, the breath, the name of God. Vairagya: loosening the grip of wanting.
That pair is the backbone of Hindu meditation; Patanjali's Yoga Sutras name the very same two. So Gita 6.5 isn't a pep talk. It's a discipline.

teach.h: THE SAME WORD AT BOTH ENDS OF THE ROPE.
teach.b: The self lifts the self by returning, day after day, and the same word stands at both ends of the rope.

how: Many Hindus practice japa, repeating a mantra or a name of God, often on a mala of 108 beads, and simply come back to it when the mind wanders; some learn Gita 6.5 by heart.

games.q: the self and how it's lifted — tap the pairs.
p: practice: coming back again and again

s: Krishna tells Arjuna the restless mind can't really be held
he agrees it's restless as the wind, then says it is held by abhyasa, practice, and vairagya, letting go (6.35).
Gita 6.5 calls the self both friend and enemy of the self
atmaiva bandhur, atmaiva ripur: the self alone is each.
the verse says exactly which self lifts which
readers differ: the mind steadying the person, or a deeper self raising a restless one.

games.q: a friend starts japa, repeating a mantra each morning, and quits after two days: 'my mind wanders, so i'm bad at it.' by Gita 6, what do you send?
o: 'wandering is the wind. coming back each time is the practice itself.'
'if your mind wanders, this path isn't for you.'
'empty your mind completely first, then start.'
games.why: Krishna admits the mind is restless as the wind, and says it is held by abhyasa, coming back, and vairagya, letting go. the return is the practice.

practice: Do what Krishna prescribes, in small. Choose one anchor: Om, or a mantra you know, like Om namah Shivaya, or the name of God you pray to; if you don't pray, your own breath. Repeat it softly.
Each time the mind runs off, and it will, that's the wind. Come back without scolding. Each return is abhyasa.

wordCard.voice: Two hundred core words: today, atman, the self, or plain oneself, in its shapes atma, atmanam, atmana, atmanah. And two that hold it steady: abhyasa, practice, and vairagya, letting go.

orig.note: Sanskrit: atman, the self, or oneself; it turns up in several shapes in Gita 6.5.

carryVoice: The line to take with you: abhyasa and vairagya. The self lifts the self by coming back, again and again.
